The Museum of Unfinished Things

I have been thinking a lot lately about the things we leave half-done and how they start to accumulate like dust in the attic of a house we no longer live in. Not the big, dramatic unfinished things, like the novel you swore you would write or the apology you never sent. Those are the ones everyone talks about. I mean the small ones. The half-read library book with a paperclip still biting its spine. The plant you bought on a Tuesday because it looked lonely in the shop window and now lives on your kitchen sill with three yellow leaves. The recipe you saved to your phone with the note “make this when you have time” and the time has never arrived.

I think if you were to follow me through my apartment you would find a museum of these things. The curator is very tired. There is a half-knitted scarf in the living room, the yarn a soft, impractical color called “mauve heather.” I bought the yarn in a craft store in 2019, before I understood that I do not actually like knitting. I like the idea of knitting. I like the way it looks in movies. I like the idea of a person who makes things with their hands while listening to the radio. The scarf is seven inches long. It will never be finished and it will never be thrown away, because throwing it away feels like admitting something about myself that I am not ready to admit.

On the desk there is a notebook with only the first three pages filled. The first page says “Ideas for when I’m stuck.” The second page has a list: 1. Walk without headphones. 2. Call my sister. 3. Learn how to make sourdough. The third page is a half-finished sketch of a coffee cup. The fourth page is blank. The notebook is a perfect object because it contains the entire human condition in three pages: intention, a list, and then the sudden realization that you can’t draw a coffee cup without it looking like a child’s drawing of a coffee cup.

I used to believe that finishing things was a moral quality. That people who finished things were better people. Now I think finishing is a kind of luck. It requires the right convergence of time, energy, interest, and a life that is not being pulled in seventeen different directions at once. Most of us live in a state of perpetual partial attention. We are always about to start, always about to finish. We live in the comma.

And yet there is a strange comfort in the unfinished. An unfinished thing is a promise you made to a future version of yourself. It is a little bridge you built across time. Even if you never cross it, the fact that it exists means you once believed you would. That belief is worth something. It is a record of hope.

I was walking home last Thursday through the market district, the one where the fruit stands spill over onto the sidewalk and the air smells like overripe bananas and diesel. I stopped at a stall where an old man was selling clocks. Not new clocks. Old clocks. Clocks with cracked glass and brass faces and hands that pointed to times that no longer existed. He had them laid out on a table like a dealer of small miracles.

“Do they work?” I asked him.

He smiled without showing his teeth. “Some of them,” he said. “Most of them tell the same time every day. The time they stopped.”

I picked up a small mantel clock, its wood dark with age. The hands were frozen at 3:17. I asked him how much.

“Fifty dollars,” he said. “Or you can take it for the story.”

I bought it for the story, which is to say I bought it for fifty dollars. I brought it home and set it on my shelf next to the half-knitted scarf. It sits there and tells me that it is always 3:17. I like that. It is a clock that refuses to participate in the tyranny of the present moment. It lives permanently in a small, quiet afternoon that happened a long time ago.

That is what unfinished things are: clocks that stopped at a particular moment and decided to stay there.

I think about my grandmother’s house when I think about this. She kept everything. Not in a hoarder way. In an archivist way. She had a box of buttons in a tin. A drawer of loose change from countries she had never visited. A shoebox of ticket stubs from movies she had seen in the 1960s. She would pull them out and tell stories about them, not because the objects were important but because the stories were. The objects were just anchors for the stories.

When she died, my mother wanted to throw everything away. I told her no. We kept the buttons. We kept the ticket stubs. We threw away the change. I still have a small tin of buttons on my dresser. I never use them. I just look at them sometimes and think about the coats they once held together.

There is a particular kind of grief that lives in unfinished things. Not the grief of loss, but the grief of possibility. The thing that could have been. The scarf could have been warm around someone’s neck on a winter morning. The sourdough could have been crusty and fragrant and the centerpiece of a dinner party. The call to my sister could have been a long, easy conversation that ended with us both laughing.

We treat unfinished things as failures, but they are also evidence. Evidence that we were alive enough to want something. That we had enough imagination to picture a future where the thing existed in the world. That is not nothing.

Sometimes I try to finish things, just to see what happens. Last month I decided to finish the scarf. I sat down with the needles and the mauve heather yarn and I knit for twenty minutes. My fingers remembered nothing. The stitches were uneven. The scarf grew by two inches. I stopped. It was not enjoyable. It was labor. It was the difference between loving the idea of a thing and loving the thing itself. I put the scarf back on the couch. It is fine there.

I think about writers who talk about the discipline of writing every day. The ritual. The blank page. I admire them. I also understand the people who write in bursts, in spurts, in stolen moments between other lives. I am the second kind. My notebooks are full of beginnings. I have three different stories started in three different notebooks, each one beginning with a woman waking up in a strange room. I think I am trying to write the same story over and over until I get it right, or until I realize I don’t want to write it at all.

Maybe the point is not to finish. Maybe the point is to keep the museum open. To keep adding to the collection. To walk through it sometimes with a cup of tea and remember who you were when you started each thing.

There is a Japanese concept called tsukumogami, the idea that objects acquire spirits after 100 years. I like to imagine that my unfinished things will eventually become spirits. The scarf will become a small, woolly ghost who drifts around apartments looking for a neck to warm. The notebook will become a shy ghost who whispers ideas to people in dreams. The clock will remain a ghost who is always 3:17 and is very proud of it.

I am not sure what to do with all of this. Part of me wants to make a purge, to have a weekend where I finish or throw away everything. Another part of me knows that I would regret it. The act of clearing out is also an act of erasing. You erase the evidence of your own wanting.

So I keep them. I keep them not out of laziness but out of love. A weird, complicated love for the versions of myself that had hope. For the Tuesday me who bought the plant. For the 2019 me who bought the yarn. For the me who sat down and wrote “Ideas for when I’m stuck” in a notebook.

If you ever visit, I will show you the museum. I will walk you through the living room and point out the scarf. I will show you the clock that is always 3:17. I will open the notebook to the page where the coffee cup looks like a child’s drawing. I will tell you the stories.

You might ask me why I don’t finish them. I will tell you I don’t know. Or I will tell you that finishing is not the point. Or I will tell you that I am waiting for the right moment. The truth is probably a mixture of all three.

There is something deeply human about living among the unfinished. It means you are still in process. It means you have not given up on the idea that things can be started, even if they are not completed. It means you believe in a future self, even if you are not entirely sure that self will show up.

I think we need more museums of unfinished things. We need spaces where we can put our half-knitted scarves and our frozen clocks and our lists of ideas. We need places where we can admit that we are not done, that we may never be done, and that that is okay.

I keep coming back to the market, to the old man with his clocks. I wonder what his story is. I wonder if he has a museum of his own at home. I wonder if he has a mantelpiece full of clocks that tell different times, each one a moment he decided to keep.

Maybe he does. Maybe we all do.

I will go home now and make tea. I will sit on the couch and look at the scarf. I will not knit. I will just look at it for a minute and remember the person who bought the yarn because it was a soft, impractical color called mauve heather. I will thank her for her optimism. I will tell her it is okay. It is enough to have started.

The clock will tick, or it will not. It will say 3:17. The plant will lose another leaf. The notebook will stay open to the blank page. And I will be here, in the middle of all of it, curating a museum that will never close, because the collection is me, and I am still being made.
